stages.title: Counting and number recognition
stages.hook: How many fingers do you have on one hand? How can you be sure you did not miss one?
explain: Counting tells us how many things there are. We say the numbers in order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
Touch each thing one time as you say a number. The last number you say tells how many there are.
A number is a symbol. The symbol 3 means three apples, three drums or three friends. Counting works the same way for everything.

steps: Touch the first mango and say 1.
Touch each next mango and say 2, then 3, then 4.
Stop. The last number you said is the answer.

analogies.home: Count the spoons when you set the table. One spoon for each person.
analogies.farm: Count the hens as they walk into the coop. Touch each one once in your head.
analogies.sport: Count the goals in a game. Each goal adds one more.
analogies.nature: Count the petals on a flower. Start at one petal and go round.

stages.mnemonic: Touch and say, touch and say. The last number is the way!
terms: A word and a symbol that tell how many.
Say numbers in order for each thing.
One of the ten number symbols: 0 to 9.

misc.wrong: Counting the same thing twice gives a bigger number.
misc.right: Touch each thing only one time. Then the last number is right.

trip.prompt: Look for pictures of people counting in different ways, such as with fingers.

questions.q: You count 5 stones. You say 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. How many stones are there?
questions.why: The last number you say tells how many. It is 5.

questions.q: What comes after 6 when we count?
questions.why: We count 6, then 7.

questions.q: What comes just before 10?
questions.why: The number before 10 is 9.

questions.q: Which symbol means three?
questions.why: The symbol 3 means three things.

questions.q: Mia counts 4 balls but touches one ball two times. Her answer is 5. What went wrong?
o: She counted one ball two times
She forgot to say numbers in order
questions.why: Touch each thing one time only. If you count one twice, the answer is too big.

questions.q: You have 8 beads in a row. You start at the other end. How many beads do you count now?
questions.why: The number of beads does not change when you count from the other end.

questions.q: How many legs does a hen have? Write a number.
questions.why: A hen has 2 legs.

questions.q: Count: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐. How many stars?
questions.why: Touch each star and count to 7.

questions.q: Put the numbers in counting order.
questions.why: We count 2, 3, 4, 5.

questions.q: Kofi has 6 pencils in a cup. He takes the pencils out and puts them in a row. How many pencils now?
questions.why: Moving things does not change how many there are.

panel.q: Ana counts 3 cups. Her friend counts the same cups and says 4. What should they do?
o: Count again, touching each cup one time
panel.why: Counting again with care finds the right answer.

panel.q: Why do we say numbers in the same order every time?
o: So everyone gets the same answer
Because it is just a rule from long ago
panel.why: A fixed order lets us all agree on how many.

panel.q: You count 10 shells in a bowl. Then you count them again and get 10. What does this tell you?
o: The shells must have changed number
You must count a third time
panel.why: Getting the same answer twice is a good check.

teach.model: Counting means saying numbers in order. You touch each thing one time. The last number you say tells how many. Like counting three apples: 1, 2, 3.

points.ask: How do I know I do not skip one?
What do I say first, second and third?
Which number do I pick at the end?

stages.title: Comparing numbers and quantities
stages.hook: You have a big pile of sweets and your friend has a small pile. How can you tell who has more without counting?
explain: We compare numbers to see which is more, less or the same. More means a bigger number. Less means a smaller number.
We can match things one to one. Put one sweet next to one sweet. The pile with sweets left over has more.
On a number line, numbers further right are bigger. 8 is bigger than 5 because it comes later when we count.

example.q: Sam has 6 marbles. Lina has 4 marbles. Who has more?
steps: Count up from 4: 5, 6. So 6 comes after 4.
example.a: Sam has more. 6 is bigger than 4.

analogies.home: Two plates of rice. The plate with more rice has the bigger pile.
analogies.farm: Two baskets of eggs. Pair each egg and see which basket has extras.
analogies.sport: The team with more goals wins the game.
analogies.sea: Two boats with fish. The boat with more fish has the bigger number.

stages.mnemonic: Right on the line is bigger, left is less. The crocodile eats the bigger one: > !
terms: A sign that points to the smaller number.

misc.wrong: A bigger pile always means a bigger number.
misc.right: A spread-out small group can look big. Count or match them to be sure.

trip.prompt: Look at the number line picture. Which way are the bigger numbers?

questions.q: Which number is the biggest?
questions.why: 9 comes later than 3, 5 and 6 when we count.

questions.q: Which number is the smallest?
questions.why: 2 comes first when we count.

questions.q: Tom has 5 apples. Zara has 8 apples. Who has fewer?
questions.why: 5 is smaller than 8, so Tom has fewer.

questions.q: Which sign makes this true? 7 __ 3
questions.why: 7 is bigger than 3. The sign opens to the bigger number: 7 > 3.

questions.q: Which is true?
questions.why: 4 and 4 are the same number.

questions.q: Row A has 9 seeds close together. Row B has 6 seeds spread far apart. Which row has more seeds?
questions.why: Spread out does not mean more. 9 is bigger than 6.

questions.q: Put the numbers from smallest to biggest.
questions.why: We count 2, 4, 7, 9. Smaller numbers come first.

questions.q: Which number is one more than 8? Write it.
questions.why: One more than 8 is 9.

questions.q: Which number is one less than 5? Write it.
questions.why: One less than 5 is 4.

questions.q: Pair each cup with one plate. 2 plates have no cup. What does this show?
o: There are more plates than cups
questions.why: Plates with no partner are left over, so plates are more.

panel.q: Ben says: "10 is smaller than 7 because 7 is a big digit." What is wrong?
o: We compare how many, not how the digit looks
panel.why: 10 is more than 7. The size of a number is how many it stands for.

panel.q: A child has 5 big stones. Another child has 7 tiny stones. Who has more stones?
o: Big stones always count as double
panel.why: We compare how many stones, not how big they are.

panel.q: Why is matching one to one a good way to compare?
o: It is always faster than counting every time
It works even before we can count
panel.why: If every item has a partner and some are left over, that group has more.

teach.model: Bigger means more. 8 is bigger than 5 because 8 things is more than 5 things. You can line up the things in pairs to see. The group with extras is bigger.

points.ask: What does bigger mean for numbers?
How can I check without counting?
Can you show me with an example?

stages.title: Addition
stages.hook: You have 3 oranges. A friend gives you 2 more. How many oranges do you have now?
explain: Adding means putting groups together to find the total. The sign + means add. The sign = means is the same as.
3 + 2 = 5 means three and two make five. You can count on: start at 3, then count 4, 5.
You can add in any order. 2 + 3 is the same as 3 + 2. Adding zero changes nothing.

example.q: There are 4 birds on a roof. 3 more birds come. How many birds now?
steps: Check with fingers: hold up 4, then 3 more.

analogies.home: 3 spoons in the drawer and 2 more on the table. Put them together: 5 spoons.
analogies.farm: 4 cows in the field and 1 more walks in. Now there are 5.
analogies.music: Clap 2 times, then clap 3 times. You clapped 5 times.
analogies.city: 2 buses are at the stop. 4 more come. Now 6 buses.

stages.mnemonic: Put together, count on. The plus sign shows two groups join!
terms: How many there are after adding.

misc.wrong: Adding always means you must count from 1 each time.
misc.right: You can start at the bigger number and count on. It is faster.

trip.prompt: Look for pictures that show adding groups together.

questions.q: What is 2 + 2?
questions.why: 2 and 2 make 4.

questions.q: What is 5 + 1?
questions.why: One more than 5 is 6.

questions.q: What is 0 + 7?
questions.why: Adding zero changes nothing.

questions.q: Which sign means add?
questions.why: The plus sign means add.

questions.q: Zoe has 3 stickers and gets 4 more. Which sum fits?
questions.why: Getting more means adding: 3 + 4.

questions.q: Which one is the same as 4 + 3?
questions.why: We can add in any order. The total stays 7.

questions.q: There are 6 ducks in a pond. 3 more swim in. How many ducks now?
questions.why: 6 + 3 = 9. Count on from 6: 7, 8, 9.

questions.q: What is 5 + 5?
questions.why: Two hands of 5 fingers make 10.

questions.q: Ali says 4 + 4 = 7. How can you check?
o: Hold up 4 fingers on each hand and count all
questions.why: 4 and 4 make 8, so Ali made a mistake. Counting all the fingers shows 8.

questions.q: Match each sum to its total.
questions.why: Add the two groups to find each total.

panel.q: You want 3 + 8. Which way is quicker?
panel.why: Start with the bigger number and count on the smaller one. It is fewer steps and the answer is the same.

panel.q: Sara adds 5 + 2 and gets 3. What did she probably do?
o: She took away instead of adding
panel.why: 5 − 2 = 3. The plus sign means put together, so the answer should be bigger than 5.

panel.q: If you add some to a group, can the total be smaller than the start?
o: No, adding makes it bigger or the same
panel.why: Adding puts more in. Adding zero keeps it the same.

teach.model: Adding means putting groups together to find how many in all. If you have 2 apples and get 3 more, you now have 5. You can count on from the first number.

points.ask: What do we do to the groups?
What do we find out?
Can you give me a picture example?

stages.title: Subtraction
stages.hook: There are 5 cakes on a plate. You eat 2. How many are left?
explain: Subtracting means taking away. The sign − means take away. What is left is the answer.
5 − 2 = 3. You can count back: start at 5, then 4, 3. Or you can cross out 2 things and count what is left.
Subtracting is the opposite of adding. If 3 + 2 = 5, then 5 − 2 = 3. They fit together like a pair.

example.q: A basket has 8 eggs. Mama uses 3 eggs. How many are left?

analogies.home: You have 6 biscuits. You share 2 with a friend. 4 are left with you.
analogies.farm: 10 chicks in the yard. 4 run into the barn. 6 are still in the yard.
analogies.sport: A team has 9 balls. 3 roll away. 6 balls are left.
analogies.sea: 7 fish in a net. 2 swim out. 5 fish stay in.

stages.mnemonic: Take away, count back. Minus makes a smaller stack!
terms: What is left, or how far apart two numbers are.

misc.wrong: Taking away always needs the answer to be bigger.
misc.right: Taking away makes the number smaller. The answer is less than where you started.

trip.prompt: Look for pictures that show taking away from a group.

questions.q: What is 4 − 1?
questions.why: Take away 1 from 4 and 3 is left.

questions.q: What is 7 − 0?
questions.why: Taking away nothing leaves the same number.

questions.q: Which sign means take away?
questions.why: The minus sign means take away.

questions.q: Lola has 9 grapes and eats 4. Which sum fits?
questions.why: Eating means taking away: 9 − 4.

questions.q: 3 + 4 = 7. Which fact goes with it?
questions.why: Taking 4 away from 7 gives back the 3.

questions.q: Is 6 − 2 bigger or smaller than 6?
questions.why: Taking something away makes less.

questions.q: There are 10 kites in the sky. 6 land. How many are still flying?
What is 8 − 8?
questions.why: Take away all 8 and nothing is left.

questions.q: Omar says 5 − 2 = 7. How can you see he is wrong?
o: Taking away should make a smaller number than 5
Minus is the same as plus
questions.why: 5 − 2 = 3. The answer 7 is bigger than 5, which cannot happen when you take away.

questions.q: Count back from 6 by ones. Put the numbers in order.
questions.why: Counting back goes 6, 5, 4, 3, 2.

panel.q: You know 4 + 5 = 9. How does that help with 9 − 5?
o: It helps only if you count again
panel.why: Subtracting undoes adding, so 9 − 5 = 4.

panel.q: A child has 5 sweets and says 5 − 7 = 2. What is the problem?
o: You cannot take 7 away from only 5
panel.why: You cannot take away more than you have. The answer cannot be 2.

panel.q: How is subtracting like adding?
panel.why: Adding puts things in, subtracting takes them out.

teach.model: Subtracting means taking some away from a group. What is left is the answer. If you have 6 sweets and eat 2, 4 are left.

points.ask: What do we do to the group?
What do we find out at the end?
Can you show me with something I can picture?

stages.title: Multiplication concepts
stages.hook: A hen has 2 legs. How many legs do 3 hens have? Is there a quick way to find out?
explain: Multiplying means making equal groups. Three groups of 2 is 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. We write this as 3 × 2 = 6.
Equal groups is the big idea. Each group must have the same number. 3 plates with 4 apples each is 3 groups of 4.
Multiplying is a quick way of adding the same number again and again. Skip counting helps: 2, 4, 6 or 5, 10, 15.

example.q: There are 4 bags. Each bag has 3 oranges. How many oranges in all?

analogies.home: Egg boxes with 2 rows of 3 eggs. 2 groups of 3 is 6 eggs.
analogies.farm: 5 cows. Each cow has 4 legs. 5 groups of 4 is 20 legs.
analogies.music: 3 drums, each with 2 sticks. That is 6 sticks.
analogies.city: 4 cars, each with 4 wheels. That is 16 wheels.

stages.mnemonic: Groups that are the same make multiplying a game. Skip count and win!
terms: Groups with the same number in each.

misc.right: The groups must be equal. Unequal groups need adding, not times.

trip.prompt: Look for pictures of dots in rows and groups.

questions.q: What is 2 + 2 + 2 as a times fact?
questions.why: There are three groups of 2, so 3 × 2.

questions.q: Which are equal groups?
o: A plate with 2, one with 5 and one with 1
A mix of apples and plates
questions.why: Each plate has the same number, so the groups are equal.

questions.q: Count in 2s: 2, 4, 6, __. What comes next?
questions.why: We add 2 each time: 6 + 2 = 8.

questions.q: Count in 5s: 5, 10, 15, __. What comes next?
A spider has 8 legs. Which sum is for 2 spiders?
questions.why: Two equal groups of 8 is 8 + 8.

questions.q: Does 2 groups of 3 give the same as 3 groups of 2?
questions.why: 3 + 3 = 6 and 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. The order does not change the answer.

questions.q: There are 3 boxes with 5 pencils in each box. How many pencils in all?
questions.why: 3 groups of 5: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15.

questions.q: What is 4 × 2?
questions.why: Four groups of 2: 2, 4, 6, 8.

questions.q: Nia has 2 bags with 3 shells and 1 bag with 5 shells. Can she write 3 × 3?
o: No, the groups are not all equal
questions.why: 3 × 3 needs three bags of 3. One bag has 5 so the groups are not equal.

questions.q: Match the picture to the times fact.
questions.why: The first number tells how many groups. The second tells how many in each group.

panel.q: Why is 5 × 0 equal to 0?
o: Five groups with nothing in them hold nothing
It is a rule with no reason
panel.why: Zero in every group means zero in all.

panel.q: Mei counts 3 groups of 4 by adding 4 + 4 + 4 and gets 12. Her friend skip counts 4, 8, 12. What can you say?
panel.why: Skip counting is a quick way to do repeated adding.

panel.q: How is multiplying linked to adding?
o: It is adding the same number again and again
It is the opposite of adding

teach.model: Multiplying means making equal groups. If there are 3 plates with 2 biscuits each, you have 3 groups of 2. That is 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 biscuits.

points.ask: What is a group?
Do the groups have to be the same?
How do I find how many in all?

stages.title: Division and sharing
stages.hook: You have 8 sweets and want to share them fairly with 2 friends. How many does each one get?
explain: Dividing means sharing into equal groups. The sign ÷ means divide. Fair sharing means everyone gets the same.
12 ÷ 3 = 4 means 12 things shared into 3 groups gives 4 in each group. You can deal them out one by one like cards.
Dividing is the opposite of multiplying. If 3 × 4 = 12, then 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Sometimes there are some left over.

example.q: Share 10 biscuits fairly between 2 children. How many does each child get?
steps: Deal out the biscuits one at a time: one to each child.
Keep going until all 10 are gone.

analogies.home: Share a bowl of 12 dates between 4 people. Each gets 3.
analogies.farm: Put 15 apples into 3 baskets. Each basket has 5.
analogies.sport: Split 10 players into 2 teams. Each team has 5.
analogies.sea: Put 8 fish into 4 buckets. Each bucket holds 2.

stages.mnemonic: Deal like cards, one for you, one for me. Same for all is fair sharing!
terms: Give each group the same amount.
What is left when things cannot be shared equally.

misc.wrong: Dividing means each person gets a different amount.
misc.right: Dividing means the groups are equal. Each one gets the same.

trip.prompt: Look for pictures showing things shared into equal groups.

questions.q: What is 6 ÷ 2?
questions.why: Share 6 into 2 equal groups: 3 each.

questions.q: Which sign means divide?
questions.why: The sign ÷ means share into equal groups.

questions.q: What does fair sharing mean?
questions.why: Dividing makes equal groups.

questions.q: Share 9 sweets between 3 children. Which sum is it?
questions.why: Sharing into equal groups is dividing.

questions.q: You know 2 × 5 = 10. Which fact goes with it?
questions.why: Dividing undoes multiplying.

questions.q: Share 7 sweets between 2 children. What happens?
o: Each gets 3 and 1 is left over
Each gets 3 and 2 are left over
questions.why: 3 + 3 = 6 and 1 is left over.

questions.q: Share 12 mangoes into 4 equal bags. How many in each bag?
Share 20 stickers between 5 children. How many for each child?
Pia says 8 ÷ 2 = 16. How can you see it is wrong?
o: Sharing makes the groups smaller than 8
questions.why: 8 shared into 2 groups gives 4 each. The answer cannot be more than 8.

questions.q: Dealing out 6 cards to 2 players. Put the steps in order.
items: Give one card to each player
Keep dealing one at a time
questions.why: We start with the total, deal evenly, then check.

panel.q: Why can 6 be shared equally between 2 but 7 cannot?
o: 7 leaves one over after two equal groups
7 cannot be put into groups of any kind at all
It can, there is no problem
panel.why: Two groups of 3 use 6. The seventh is left over.

panel.q: How is dividing like taking away?
o: It is never like taking away
You can keep taking away the same amount
panel.why: Take 2 away from 6 again and again: you can do it 3 times, so 6 ÷ 2 = 3.

panel.q: A child says: "12 ÷ 3 and 12 ÷ 4 give the same answer." What do you say?
panel.why: More groups means fewer in each group.

teach.model: Dividing means sharing into equal groups so everyone gets the same. If you share 8 sweets between 4 children, each child gets 2.

points.ask: What does fair sharing mean?
How do I do the sharing?
Can you show me with sweets?

stages.title: Shapes and patterns
stages.hook: Look around the room. What shapes can you find? What makes a circle different from a square?
explain: Shapes have names. A circle is round with no corners. A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners. A square has 4 equal sides and 4 corners. A rectangle has 4 sides and 4 corners too.
A pattern is something that repeats. Red, blue, red, blue is a pattern. The part that repeats is called the unit.
To find what comes next in a pattern, find the part that repeats. Then carry on the same way.

steps: Look at the colours: red, blue, red, blue, red.
The unit that repeats is red then blue.

analogies.home: A plate is a circle. A window is often a rectangle. A tile can be a square.
analogies.city: A road sign can be a triangle. A wheel is a circle.
analogies.music: A drum beat can be a pattern: loud, soft, loud, soft.
analogies.nature: A sunflower seed head makes a pattern of spirals.

stages.mnemonic: Circle round, triangle three, square has four sides: one, two, three, four!
terms: A straight edge of a shape.
Something that repeats in a way you can predict.
The part of a pattern that repeats.

misc.wrong: A square and a rectangle can never have anything in common.
misc.right: A square is a special rectangle. It has 4 corners and its sides are all equal.

trip.prompt: Look for shapes in buildings from different countries.

questions.q: How many sides does a triangle have?
questions.why: Tri means three. A triangle has 3 sides.

questions.q: Which shape has no corners?
questions.why: A circle is round, so it has no corners.

questions.q: How many corners does a square have?
questions.why: A square has 4 sides and 4 corners.

questions.q: A door is usually which shape?
questions.why: Most doors are long with 4 corners, so rectangles.

questions.q: What is the next shape? ⬛⚪⬛⚪⬛ __
questions.why: Square and circle take turns. After a square comes a circle.

questions.q: Which pattern repeats the unit "clap, stamp"?
questions.why: The unit clap, stamp comes round again and again.

questions.q: Which is the odd one out? Square, rectangle, triangle, circle
o: It depends on what you look for
questions.why: A circle has no corners. A triangle has 3 sides while the others have 4 or none. Different rules give different odd ones.

questions.q: How many sides do 2 triangles have in all?
questions.why: Each triangle has 3 sides. 3 + 3 = 6.

questions.q: Match the shape to what it has.
questions.why: Each shape has its own sides and corners.

questions.q: Put the steps for carrying on a pattern in order.
questions.why: First look, then find the repeating unit, then carry on with it.

panel.q: Is a square also a rectangle?
o: Yes, it has 4 corners and straight sides
panel.why: A square is a rectangle that also has all sides equal.

panel.q: A pattern goes: 2, 4, 6, 8. What comes next?
panel.why: The pattern adds 2 each time. 8 + 2 = 10.

panel.q: A child says a triangle can have 4 sides. What do you say?
o: No, if it has 4 sides it is not a triangle
panel.why: Three sides is what makes a triangle.

teach.model: A shape has a name from its sides and corners. A triangle has 3 sides. A pattern is something that repeats, like red, blue, red, blue. To carry on a pattern, find the part that repeats.

points.ask: What makes a shape different from another shape?
What is a pattern?
Can you give me an example?

stages.title: Measurement and time
stages.hook: Is your pencil longer than your hand? How could you find out without a ruler?
explain: We measure to find out how long, how heavy or how much. Length is how long something is. We can use a ruler, or hands and feet.
Always start at the zero. Line the object up with the start of the ruler. Then read where it ends.
Time is measured with clocks. There are 60 minutes in 1 hour and 24 hours in 1 day. 7 days make a week. The short hand shows hours and the long hand shows minutes.

example.q: A pencil starts at 0 on a ruler and ends at 12 on the centimetre side. How long is it?
steps: Read the number: 12. The unit is centimetres.

analogies.home: Measure a table with your hand spans. Say 6 spans long.
analogies.farm: Weigh a bag of rice. It is 5 kilograms.
analogies.sport: A race on a track. The clock shows who is first.
analogies.music: A song is 3 minutes long. Count the minutes on the clock.

stages.mnemonic: Start at zero, then look. Read the number from the book of the ruler!
terms: A small unit of length, written cm.

misc.wrong: You can start measuring from any mark on the ruler.
misc.right: Start at zero. Otherwise the answer will be wrong.

trip.prompt: Look for the marks on a ruler. What do the small lines mean?

questions.q: Which tool measures length?
questions.why: A ruler is made to measure how long something is.

questions.q: Which tool tells the time?
questions.why: A clock shows hours and minutes.

questions.q: How many days are in a week?
questions.why: A week has 7 days.

questions.q: How many hours are in a day?
questions.why: One whole day and night is 24 hours.

questions.q: A rope is 3 hand spans long when Ana measures. When her taller dad measures, he gets 2. Why?
questions.why: Hand spans are different sizes. Standard units like cm give the same answer for everyone.

questions.q: A pencil starts at 2 on the ruler and ends at 9. Is it 9 long?
questions.why: The pencil does not start at 0. 9 − 2 = 7.

questions.q: Which is the longest time?
questions.why: 1 hour is 60 minutes.

questions.q: How many minutes are in 1 hour?
questions.why: There are 60 minutes in 1 hour.

questions.q: A pencil is 15 cm and a crayon is 9 cm. How many cm longer is the pencil?
Put these in order from the shortest time to the longest.
questions.why: A minute is shorter than an hour. A day is 24 hours and a week is 7 days.

panel.q: Why do people all over the world use the same units, like centimetres?
o: So that everyone measures the same way
Because hands are all the same
panel.why: Standard units mean a measurement means the same thing everywhere.

panel.q: School starts at 8 and ends at 1 (5 hours later). Which tool helps you see how long the day is?
panel.why: A clock measures time.

panel.q: You measure a book as 20 cm. Then you measure a longer book as 15 cm. What might be wrong?
o: The longer book was not lined up at zero
panel.why: Wrong starting points give wrong answers. Check the 0.

teach.model: To measure length, put the start of the object at 0 on the ruler. Then read the number where the object ends. For example, a pencil that ends at 12 is 12 centimetres long.

points.ask: Where do I begin on the ruler?
Then what do I do?
What do I say after the number?

stages.title: Introduction to charts and data
stages.hook: Your class likes different fruits. How could you show which fruit is the favourite so everyone can see?
explain: Data is information we collect. We can ask questions and count the answers. A tally marks each answer with a line: ||||.
A chart shows data as a picture. In a picture chart, each little picture stands for one thing. In a bar chart, taller bars mean bigger numbers.
Reading a chart means finding the biggest, the smallest and how many. We can then answer questions like which is most popular.

example.q: In a class, 5 children like mangoes, 3 like bananas and 2 like oranges. Which fruit is most popular?
steps: Make a tally: mangoes 5, bananas 3, oranges 2.
Compare the numbers: 5 is the biggest.

analogies.home: Tally how many red, green and blue cups are in the kitchen.
analogies.farm: Count the cows, hens and goats. Draw a picture chart.
analogies.sport: Tally goals scored by each player. The tallest bar scored most.
analogies.nature: Count birds that visit a tree each day this week.

stages.mnemonic: Four lines and a slash make five. Counting data makes charts come alive!
terms: Marks used to count as we go.
A block on a chart, taller means more.

misc.wrong: The tallest bar means the best thing.
misc.right: The tallest bar means the most. It tells how many, not what is best.

trip.prompt: Look at the bar charts. Find the tallest and the shortest bar.

questions.q: What is data?
o: A way of drawing straight lines
questions.why: Data is the facts we gather by counting or asking.

questions.q: A bar chart has a tall bar for cats and a short bar for fish. Which pet has more?
questions.why: The taller bar means more.

questions.q: Tally marks: four lines with a slash across them, then one more line. How many is that?
questions.why: Four lines plus a slash is 5, plus 1 more makes 6.

questions.q: A picture chart uses one 🍎 for 1 child. Mango has 🥭🥭🥭 and apple has 🍎🍎. Which is more?
questions.why: 3 pictures is more than 2 pictures.

questions.q: Why do we make charts?
o: To see and compare data quickly
questions.why: A chart shows the facts so we can answer questions at a glance.

questions.q: A chart says 5 children like red, 5 like blue and 2 like green. Which is true?
questions.why: 5 and 5 are the same. Green has 2, the fewest.

questions.q: Pets: 4 dogs, 3 cats, 2 birds. How many pets in all?
Bar chart: red 7, blue 4. How many more like red than blue?
Match the word to its meaning.
pairs: Marks to count as you go
questions.why: These words are used when we make and read charts.

questions.q: Two friends make a chart of the same class. Ana has 6 for football and Ben has 7. Why might they differ?
o: One of them counted wrongly or missed a child
questions.why: When counts differ we check by counting again.

panel.q: A bar chart shows 8 for tea and 4 for juice. Does this mean tea is better?
o: Yes, because the bar for tea is taller
No, only that more people chose it
panel.why: A chart shows how many, not what is better.

panel.q: What can go wrong if you forget to count one child?
o: The chart will show a wrong number
panel.why: Missing data makes the picture wrong.

panel.q: Why do bars on a chart start at zero?
o: So the bars look as tall as possible
So the bars can be small
panel.why: If bars do not start at zero, a small gap can look huge.

teach.model: A bar chart shows how many of each thing. A taller bar means more. To read it, find the bar you want and look at its number. For example, if the mango bar is tallest, mango is most popular.

points.ask: What do the bars show?
How do I tell which is most?
Can you give an example?
